# Lecture 3 — Isomorphisms and Homomorphisms

## 1. Motivation: When Are Two Groups "The Same"?

Consider the following two groups:

**$`G_1`$:** The set $`\{1, -1, i, -i\} \subset \mathbb{C}^*`$ under multiplication (the 4th roots of unity).

**$`G_2`$:** The cyclic subgroup $`\langle \rho \rangle \leq S_4`$ generated by the 4-cycle $`\rho = (1\,2\,3\,4)`$, i.e., $`1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 1`$.

The elements of $`G_2`$ are $`\{e, \rho, \rho^2, \rho^3\}`$ with $`\rho^4 = e`$.

Both groups have order 4, and both have the same multiplication table (up to relabeling elements):

| | $`e`$ | $`\rho`$ | $`\rho^2`$ | $`\rho^3`$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $`e`$ | $`e`$ | $`\rho`$ | $`\rho^2`$ | $`\rho^3`$ |
| $`\rho`$ | $`\rho`$ | $`\rho^2`$ | $`\rho^3`$ | $`e`$ |
| $`\rho^2`$ | $`\rho^2`$ | $`\rho^3`$ | $`e`$ | $`\rho`$ |
| $`\rho^3`$ | $`\rho^3`$ | $`e`$ | $`\rho`$ | $`\rho^2`$ |

This matches the multiplication table of $`G_1`$ under the correspondence $`1 \leftrightarrow e`$, $`i \leftrightarrow \rho`$, $`-1 \leftrightarrow \rho^2`$, $`-i \leftrightarrow \rho^3`$.

## 2. Isomorphisms

**Definition.** An **isomorphism** from a group $`G_1`$ to a group $`G_2`$ is a map $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$ that is:
1. **Bijective** (one-to-one and onto), and
2. **Multiplicative:** $`f(x \cdot y) = f(x) \cdot f(y)`$ for all $`x, y \in G_1`$.

(The multiplication on the left is in $`G_1`$; on the right, in $`G_2`$.)

**Definition.** Two groups $`G_1`$ and $`G_2`$ are **isomorphic**, written $`G_1 \cong G_2`$, if there exists an isomorphism $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$.

**Example.** The map $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$ defined by $`f(i^k) = \rho^k`$ is an isomorphism. It is:
- Bijective: sends $`\{1, i, -1, -i\}`$ to $`\{e, \rho, \rho^2, \rho^3\}`$ bijectively.
- Multiplicative: $`f(i^j \cdot i^k) = f(i^{j+k}) = \rho^{j+k} = \rho^j \cdot \rho^k = f(i^j) \cdot f(i^k)`$.

### Cyclic Groups

**Definition.** A group $`G`$ is **cyclic** if there exists an element $`g \in G`$ (a **generator**) such that $`G = \langle g \rangle`$, i.e., every element of $`G`$ is a power of $`g`$.

**Theorem.** Any two cyclic groups of the same order $`n`$ are isomorphic.

*Proof sketch.* If $`G_1 = \langle x_1 \rangle`$ and $`G_2 = \langle x_2 \rangle`$ both have order $`n`$, define $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$ by $`f(x_1^k) = x_2^k`$. Since both generators have order $`n`$, this is well-defined (if $`x_1^j = x_1^k`$ then $`n \mid j - k`$, so $`x_2^j = x_2^k`$). Bijectivity follows similarly. Multiplicativity: $`f(x_1^j x_1^k) = f(x_1^{j+k}) = x_2^{j+k} = x_2^j x_2^k = f(x_1^j)f(x_1^k)`$. $`\square`$

**Example (infinite groups).** The map $`f: (\mathbb{R}, +) \to (\mathbb{R}_{>0}, \times)`$ defined by $`f(x) = e^x`$ is an isomorphism. It is bijective (log is the inverse) and satisfies $`f(x + y) = e^{x+y} = e^x e^y = f(x)f(y)`$.

## 3. The Klein Four-Group $`V_4`$

The **Klein four-group** is a group of order 4 with every non-identity element having order 2. It is **not** cyclic (a cyclic group of order 4 has an element of order 4).

**Realization 1 (in $`S_4`$):** Let

```math
\tau_1 = (1\,2)(3\,4), \quad \tau_2 = (1\,3)(2\,4), \quad \tau_3 = \tau_1 \tau_2 = (1\,4)(2\,3).
```

Then $`V_4 = \{e, \tau_1, \tau_2, \tau_3\}`$ with multiplication: $`\tau_i^2 = e`$ and any two distinct $`\tau_i, \tau_j`$ multiply to give the third.

**Realization 2 (in $`\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})`$):**

```math
V_4 = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}.
```

Both realizations have the same multiplication table, so they are isomorphic.

**$`V_4 \not\cong \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}`$:** The cyclic group $`\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}`$ contains elements of order 4 (e.g., $`i`$). But $`V_4`$ has no element of order 4 — every non-identity element squares to $`e`$. Since isomorphisms preserve element orders, they cannot be isomorphic.

## 4. Testing for Isomorphism

If $`G_1 \cong G_2`$, then necessarily:
1. $`|G_1| = |G_2|`$ (same cardinality).
2. $`G_1`$ is abelian $`\iff`$ $`G_2`$ is abelian.
3. For each $`n`$, $`G_1`$ and $`G_2`$ have the same number of elements of order $`n`$.

These are **necessary** but not always **sufficient** conditions.

## 5. Automorphisms

**Definition.** An **automorphism** of a group $`G`$ is an isomorphism $`f: G \xrightarrow{\sim} G`$ (from $`G`$ to itself).

The set of all automorphisms of $`G`$ forms a group:

```math
\mathrm{Aut}(G) = \{ f: G \xrightarrow{\sim} G \mid f \text{ is an isomorphism} \}
```

under composition. One must verify:
- Composition of isomorphisms is an isomorphism. ✓
- Identity map is an automorphism. ✓
- Inverse of an isomorphism is an isomorphism (exercise). ✓

## 6. Homomorphisms

Isomorphisms require bijectivity. We can relax this:

**Definition.** A **homomorphism** from group $`G_1`$ to group $`G_2`$ is a map $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$ satisfying

```math
f(x \cdot y) = f(x) \cdot f(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y \in G_1.
```

Every isomorphism is a homomorphism; the converse is false in general.

**Examples:**

1. **Determinant map:** $`\det: \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^*`$ defined by $`A \mapsto \det(A)`$.\
   This is a homomorphism because $`\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)`$. It is **not** an isomorphism (not injective; also $`\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})`$ is non-abelian for $`n \geq 2`$ while $`\mathbb{R}^*`$ is abelian).

2. **Trivial homomorphism:** For any groups $`G_1, G_2`$, the map $`f(g) = e_{G_2}`$ for all $`g \in G_1`$ is always a homomorphism.

3. **Inclusion:** The embedding $`S_k \hookrightarrow S_n`$ (extending permutations by fixing extra letters) is an injective homomorphism that is not surjective (for $`k < n`$).

4. **Parity map:** $`f: \mathbb{Z} \to S_2 = \{e, \tau\}`$ defined by
   ```math
   f(n) = \begin{cases} e & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \\ \tau & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}\end{cases}
   ```
   is a homomorphism: even + even = even, odd + odd = even, even + odd = odd. ✓

## 7. The Image of a Homomorphism

**Definition.** For a homomorphism $`f: G_1 \to G_2`$, the **image** is

```math
\mathrm{Im}(f) = \{ f(x) : x \in G_1 \} \subseteq G_2.
```

The image is a **subgroup** of $`G_2`$. (It is closed under multiplication, contains $`e_{G_2} = f(e_{G_1})`$, and contains inverses $`f(g)^{-1} = f(g^{-1})`$.)

An isomorphism is a homomorphism where $`\mathrm{Im}(f) = G_2`$ (surjective) and the map is injective.
